- Model consistently overestimates early in the 30-day forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then gradually underestimates later days.
- Forecasts show a persistent upward bias relative to true outcomes, particularly when the true values dip sharply (e.g., after 75–80 range).
- After a sharp spike in true values (e.g., 79–80), model forecasts overshoot and remain elevated longer than warranted — suggesting delayed mean reversion or lagged response.
- Model fails to capture sudden downward corrections in true values, especially when true values drop below 70–72 after a peak.
- Forecasts tend to be smoother than true values, underestimating volatility and abrupt reversals.
- Model exhibits “mean reversion bias” — it overcorrects downward after a spike, then undercorrects upward, creating a lagged pattern.
- When true values are below 70, model forecasts remain above 70 for multiple days, indicating a persistent upward bias in low-price regimes.
- Forecasts are overly optimistic in the first 10 days, then become increasingly pessimistic — suggesting a misaligned horizon for short-term volatility.
